title: Lyten to acquire insolvent battery cell manufacturer Morrow Batteries - electrive.com
content:
US battery developer Lyten is now seeking to acquire the insolvent Norwegian battery cell manufacturer Morrow Batteries, after acquiring Swedish battery maker Northvolt. If the deal goes through, Morrow's battery technology activities could continue to be based at the company's site in Arendal.
Morrow's battery factory in Arendal, Norway.
Image: Morrow Batteries
Lyten has signed a letter of intent to acquire Morrow Batteries, in collaboration with Innovation Norway —Norway’s state-owned economic development and investment bank— and Morrow’s insolvency administrators. The
Norwegian battery specialist
initiated insolvency proceedings
earlier this year
for Morrow Batteries ASA, Morrow Technologies AS, and Morrow Industrialisation Center AS, and declared insolvency in early summer. Morrow opened a smaller industrial plant for
LFP battery cells in 2024
, and stated in June this year that it aimed to salvage at least part of its operations. These prospects now appear promising with the recently signed letter of intent from US battery developer Lyten.
Bidding process with multiple interested parties
According to their statements, the insolvency administrators and Innovation Norway had been negotiating with several bidders and finally selected Lyten as the preferred bidder. The three partners have agreed to keep the details of the letter of intent confidential.
Leon Bakkebø, Executive Vice President at Innovation Norway and responsible for financing and banking, stated: “As a secured creditor, our priority throughout the process has been to maximise value recovery and reduce execution risk.” He said they support the trustee’s decision to proceed with Lyten “because their proposal provides the strongest overall combination of financial recovery, transaction certainty and industrial credibility.” The executive further noted that, if completed, “the transaction could also create a foundation for future battery-related activity in Arendal.”
70 jobs secured in the short term
Lyten is already familiar with the acquisition of insolvent Nordic battery makers from its acquisition of the r
emaining assets of Swedish battery manufacturer Northvolt
. Christian Bohne, the lawyer administering Morrow’s insolvency estate, explained that the goal is to preserve value and seek a solution for the company’s continued existence. He pointed out that employees have been severely affected by the insolvency. “Under demanding circumstances, they have made an important and highly valued contribution to the work to continue battery production in the Arendal region. Their commitment has been instrumental in enabling us to enter into this agreement”
In the short term, Bohne said the process secures around 70 jobs until autumn. In the long term, several hundred jobs at Morrow and orders for local material and service providers could be safeguarded. However, the insolvency administrator also warns that there are circumstances and conditions beyond their control that must be met before the transaction can be completed. Nevertheless, Bohne said, “Although we do not yet know whether those circumstances can be met, I am optimistic about Lyten’s ability to execute”
Lyten aims to establish European production base
Dan Cook, CEO and co-founder of Lyten, sees significant potential in Europe. He pointed out, “Europe has entered a sustained period of infrastructure investment, and batteries are now an important part of this critical infrastructure.” Lyten aims to build a financially robust and scalable production base for batteries and energy storage in Europe, coupling technologies, supply chains, and production sites in the USA and Europe. “The Morrow team has built a business aligned with this strategy, making the assets a strong strategic fit for Lyten in Europe,” said Cook.
According to Lyten, the company is evaluating the expansion of the Morrow site into a potential “Lyten Industrial Hub.” The US company said it should be able to integrate battery production, upstream and downstream activities in the energy storage value chain, and industrial activities to support other critical sectors—including AI data centres, mobility, and defence. Lyten also plans a similar hub in Skellefteå at the former Northvolt site.
Northvolt and Morrow Batteries were long regarded as two of the few companies capable of producing battery cells in Europe but were unable to sustain activities. While Northvolt struggled with production quality during its ramp-up phase, Morrow Batteries fell victim to its small size in a consolidating market. The plant opened in summer 2024 at its headquarters in Arendal for the production of prismatic LFP cells with an annual capacity of just 1 GWh—far too small to supply a major car manufacturer. This capacity is sufficient for only around 25,000 small cars with a 40-kWh battery. For comparison, Volkswagen’s subsidiary PowerCo states that its
new cell factory in Salzgitter
has an annual capacity of 20 GWh, enough for around 250,000 small cars.
Morrow lacked investors for expansion to 43 GWh
Morrow Batteries was also targeting the construction of such a gigafactory. The Norwegian company had planned to expand the Arendal site in four stages to eventually reach 43 GWh. But this never materialised due to a lack of investors. Even the ramp-up of the existing 1-GWh plant proved to be a significant challenge, and the cell factory never achieved series production. As recently as January 2026—nearly a year and a half after the plant’s opening—Morrow Batteries stated that it was now ready for series production but was adopting a “partnership-based approach,” seeking long-term investments and strategic alliances to accelerate technology validation and secure offtake agreements. Morrow Batteries’ management commented on the insolvency in June, stating that the background was complex. “The company has been operating in an early and capital‑intensive industrialisation phase, while at the same time the global battery market has become more competitive with oversupply and resulting price pressure. In addition, increased capital costs, delays in the industrialisation process, and a more restrained investment market have made it significantly more difficult to secure financing.”

title: Forge Nano breaks ground for North Carolina gigafactory – Batteries International
content: Forge Nano has broken ground on its 3GWh ‘America Battery Gigafactory’ in North Carolina, which it said will become a key link in the domestic battery supply chain. The company, which makes semiconductors and batteries for commercial and defence customers, announced the move at its existing Morrisville facility on August 19. Forge Nano said Morrisville, backed by $100 million in federal funding from the US Department of Energy, will expand from 100,000 ft 2 to nearly 315,000ft 2 and produce some 150 million battery cells each year. Samsung SDI is supporting Forge Nano at the Morrisville plant, providing operational and manufacturing expertise. Once operational, the plant is expected to manufacture Samsung SDI battery cells alongside Forge Nano’s existing cell products. Samsung SDI has also entered into a conditional procurement agreement to buy cells manufactured at the plant starting in 2028, while Forge Nano will be a contract manufacturer and an authorised distributor of the cells in the US market. Both firms also plan to incorporate Forge Nano’s proprietary Atomic Armor nano-coating tech into future Samsung SDI battery products. The partnership was strengthened last July with a $20 million strategic investment by Samsung SDI in Forge Nano, including $10 million in Forge Nano’s Series D financing and $10 million in the company’s PIPE (private investment in public equity) — financing associated with its planned public listing. Forge Nano has also agreed to merge with special purpose acquisition company Archimedes Tech SPAC Partners II . Paul Lichty, CEO of Forge Nano, said the company is combining its technology with world-class manufacturing expertise, federal support and North Carolina’s growing advanced manufacturing ecosystem to bring critical battery production to the US. “America’s battery gigafactory will give defence, aerospace and commercial customers access to advanced battery cells manufactured here at home, at the scale needed to compete globally.” The post Forge Nano breaks ground for North Carolina gigafactory appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Clarios secures low-carbon lead supply deal with Boliden – Batteries International
content: Clarios has agreed a major deal to source low-carbon lead for its battery manufacturing plants in Europe, the Middle East and Africa from Swedish mining and metals company Boliden. Clarios confirmed the agreement on August 24, saying that Boliden’s low-carbon lead, processed from mined ore, is smelted in “highly energy efficient Nordic facilities mainly powered by fossil-free energy”. This results in a cradle-to-gate footprint below 1kg CO₂ per kg of lead, which corresponds to nearly half the emissions of other primary lead smelters in Europe, which Clarios said average 1,82kg CO₂/kg Pb. Using low-carbon lead also lowers Clarios’ carbon footprint and enables its customers to reduce their Scope 3 emissions. The low-voltage battery solutions major and owner of the VARTA Automotive brand said the Boliden supply partnership — financial details of which were not disclosed — fills an important gap. More than 75% of the lead used for production in the EMEA comes from recycled end-of-life batteries. Clarios operates the industry’s largest closed-loop battery recycling network globally with more than 8,000 recycled batteries per hour, returning valuable materials to the production cycle. Emissions reduction To meet the remaining lead demand, Clarios EMEA sources low-carbon primary lead from selected partners like Boliden. The carbon footprint of modern vehicles, regardless of the powertrain, is largely determined by the components used, Clarios said. Boliden’s low-carbon lead represents an important contribution to Clarios EMEA’s efforts to reduce emissions along the value chain, including both recycled and primary raw materials. According to Clarios, its low-voltage batteries are installed in one of three vehicles on the road globally — powering conventional, hybrid and electric vehicles. Christian Rosenkranz, VP for EMEA industry and government relations at Clarios, said strategic partnerships with trusted suppliers like Boliden were crucial for the battery giant’s path to greater sustainability. “Our mission is clear: To power the future of transportation with the world’s best batteries, produced as sustainably as possible. Our low-voltage batteries are essential for powering advanced technologies in today’s vehicles and supporting the mobility solutions of the future.” ‘Responsible choices’ Sales manager for lead at Boliden, Saga Mills, said: “We strive to lead the way in sustainable metal production, and we actively encourage our partners to be part of that journey toward a more responsible future. “Clarios’ commitment to using low-carbon lead demonstrates how responsible choices throughout the value chain lead to immediate footprint reductions.” The deal with Boliden comes three months after Clarios formally completed its acquisition of three lead battery recycling plants in Europe from Ecobat. That was followed in June with the announcement that the company had produced its 100-millionth AGM battery, which rolled off the production line in Zwickau, Germany. title: Shein's Stock Market Debut: Pressure on Supplier Networks
content:
Shein's Stock Market Debut: Pressure on Supplier Networks
Prioritise Us
on Google
Shein is targeting the Hong Kong Stock Exchange with a US$27bn valuation. Credit: Shein
Shein is making its Hong Kong stock market debut, but supply chain concerns and ongoing scrutiny has the company targeting a lower valuation than expected
Global ecommerce platform Shein rose to prominence in the late 2010s and early 2020s, becoming a major player in how consumers buy clothing.
With this, there has been growing demand for the site, alongside rising scrutiny for the way it operates.
Now, Shein is making its debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange, targeting a US$27bn valuation.
The lesson for online retailers is that visibility and contingency plans are crucial for the bottom line, including for situations where a supplier becomes unusable because of new regulatory or ethical concerns coming to light.
Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK
The rise of Shein
Initially set up in 2008 by Chris Xu (Xu Yangtian), Shein began its worldwide operations in 2012, initially selling wedding dresses. Now, it sells around the world, offering apparel and products at an affordable price. A core aim is to make fashion accessible to all, using a digital-first approach to
meet its customers
head-on.
It uses technology throughout its entire process, relying on social media and trends to stay informed of consumer demand. Its digital supply chain aims to deliver products to customers around the world at a fast-paced manner, ordering in small batches and tracking sales at all times.
The company grew significantly in 2020, driven by closed retailers amid the COVID-19 pandemic and bored consumers looking to rejuvenate their look. It reported US$10bn in revenue in 2020, and was the world's largest online-only fashion firm.
Since then, the company has continued to grow – but so has its
public scrutiny
. In 2024, Shein attempted to become listed on the London Stock Exchange for an initial public offering (IPO), following a failed attempt at the New York Stock Exchange. Public scrutiny and policy queries led to this being a failed attempt, with heavy concerns regarding the standards of care throughout its supply chain.
Now, the organisation will list itself on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September, with a valuation of approximately US$27bn. This low number has proven to be a shock to many analysts, as the company reached a private-market valuation of almost US$100bn in 2022.
"The US$73bn question for Shein is how much
poor supply chain visibility
can ultimately cost a business," explains Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK.
Ben Wright, Managing Partner at Argon & Co UK
"Its fall from a valuation of almost US$100bn at its 2022 peak to around US$27bn today cannot be attributed to supply chain concerns alone. But the scrutiny surrounding its sourcing and labour practices shows that supply chain transparency is now an investor issue as much as an operational one."
The hidden risks
Though ecommerce has skyrocketed in recent years, there has also become a greater awareness of ethics and sustainability. Consumers want reliable and fast delivery of products, but they are also prioritising organisations with transparent supply chain operations and clear sustainability initiatives.
Much of the scrutiny facing Shein is its lack of visibility and the implications which come with
fast-fashion
– particularly as Shein's prices are as low as they are. While it still has a relatively large market – 273 million active customers in 160 markets throughout 2025 – investors have greater concerns.
For a company with as much scrutiny as Shein has, investing in it is a risk – does it still have a capacity for growth, or have new standards meant that the retailer has reached its peak? If so, investors could see less benefit in taking that chance.
In the first three months of 2026, Shein faced a net loss of US$99m, following its US$395m profit in 2025. Much of this has been a result of lacking clarity across supplier base and ethics of production.
“Shein’s tumble in valuation should be a warning to e-commerce firms that investors are really laser-focused on the story behind the growth story," Ben tells Supply Chain Digital.
“Its valuation decline can’t be attributed to supply chain concerns alone, but for e-commerce businesses built on complex, global supplier networks, it does show that issues around sourcing, governance, and transparency are now investor issues as much as operational ones.
Chris Xu, CEO of SHEIN, founded the company in 2008.
“Before, e-commerce firms like Shein and Boohoo were rewarded for scale, speed and low prices. But now, investors also want evidence that these models are sustainable. Technology and AI are making much greater supply chain visibility possible, which means investors are much less tolerant of companies that can’t answer fundamental questions about where their products come from, whether
child labour
is used, and under what conditions workers are living.
“The lesson for online retailers is that visibility and contingency plans are crucial for the bottom line, including for situations where a supplier becomes unusable because of new regulatory or ethical concerns coming to light.”
Key facts
Shein is targeting a US$27bn valuation on the Hong Kong stock exchange
The company began in 2008
In 2020, Shein reported a US$10bn revenue
Shein has faced a net loss of US$99m in Q1 2026
Meeting modern standards
Though Shein has a
dedicated sustainability strategy
, evoluSHEIN, with a focus on empowering people, driving resilience and reducing waste, it is generally deemed unethical and unsustainable. Its introduction of cheap items, heavy use of synthetic materials, encouragement of hyper-consumption and low durability contribute to high levels of waste.
Ethical consumerism is growing, as more shoppers recognise their impact on the planet. The 2026 E-Commerce Trends Report by DHL found that 35% of shoppers have abandoned an online purchase due to a lack of sustainability credentials.
Though the LSE missed out on the IPO, therefore potentially putting it at a disadvantage in competitiveness with Hong Kong, it is demonstrating its focus on governance, responsible sourcing and scrutiny.

title: DHL Lands New SAS Ground Handling Deal in Manchester
content:
DHL Lands New SAS Ground Handling Deal in Manchester
Prioritise Us
on Google
The new agreement between DHL and SAS will run for three years (Image source: Getty Images/Kirillm)
David Johnson of DHL Supply Chain explains “huge team effort”, as a new three-year ground handling partnership with SAS at Manchester Airport is launched
DHL Supply Chain has been appointed as SAS Scandinavian Airlines' ground handling partner at Manchester Airport, as part of a new three-year partnership announced on 25 August 2026.
The contract will support up to five SAS flights a day, covering the airline's operations between the UK, Scandinavia and beyond. DHL will provide baggage operations, customer service, aircraft loading, dispatch and pushback.
The speed here is something to note: DHL completed the mobilisation in 30 days, standing up a
live aviation operation
while maintaining service continuity throughout.
A fast-growing corner of DHL's supply chain business
Ground handling sits within DHL Supply Chain's wider aviation and travel portfolio, which the company positions around bringing a logistics mindset to airport operations. It applies the same principles of efficiency, visibility and process discipline it uses across contract logistics more broadly.
The SAS deal is not an isolated case. Earlier this year in April,
DHL Supply Chain was appointed by Air France-KLM
to deliver full ground handling services at London Gatwick, supporting the airline's new route to Paris Charles de Gaulle, and covering a similar scope of baggage, aircraft turnaround and dispatch work, alongside cabin cleaning. Taken together, the two contracts show the way the company is steadily building out its airport footprint across the UK.
At a Glance: DHL Supply Chain and SAS at Manchester Airport:
supports up to five SAS flights a day between the UK, Scandinavia and beyond
covers baggage operations, customer service, aircraft loading, dispatch and pushback
runs for three years under the new agreement
reflects a 30-day mobilisation from signing to live operation
follows DHL's April 2026 ground handling contract with Air France-KLM at London Gatwick.
DHL positions itself within aviation and aerospace logistics more broadly as a Lead Logistics Partner capable of managing supplier relationships and coordinating complex, multi-tier supply chains for airlines, OEMs,
engine manufacturers
and suppliers alike. Its reach extends well beyond ground handling into spare parts logistics and Aircraft on Ground support.
DHL Supply Chain describes itself as the world's largest contract logistics specialist and its aviation and travel division applies that scale to ground operations specifically, combining
technology, data and process
discipline with the aim of improving on-time performance and passenger experience for airline customers. Manchester Airport, which is the UK's third-busiest by passenger volume, adds another significant hub to that growing UK footprint.
Why mobilisation speed matters
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics at DHL Supply Chain UKI, explains how the 30-day mobilisation demonstrates the operational capability behind the contract.
Mobilising a new operation in just 30 days required a huge team effort and demonstrates the agility and expertise of our aviation teams.
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics, DHL Supply Chain UKI
Ground handling has a narrow margin for error. A late bag run, a slow pushback or a delayed loading sequence can cascade into missed slots and knock-on disruption across an airline's wider schedule, which is why airlines increasingly treat their choice of ground handler as a supply chain decision, not just an airport formality.
David Johnson, Interim MD, Healthcare & Specialist Logistics, DHL Supply Chain UKI (Image source: David Johnson via LinkedIn)
The SAS side of the equation
Hans Henrik Spangenberg, MD SAS Ground Handling International, points to Manchester's role as a UK gateway connecting customers to Scandinavia and SAS' wider international network. Crediting DHL's
operational expertise
and speed of mobilisation, he calls the partnership "a smooth transition," adding that SAS looks forward to continuing the collaboration.
SAS has operated as Scandinavia's leading airline since 1946, running hubs at Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm. The airline serves more than 25 million passengers and transports 55,000 tonnes of cargo annually across 135 destinations in Europe, the US and Asia, and joined the SkyTeam alliance in September 2024.
This latest deal follows DHL's April 2026 ground handling contract with Air France-KLM at London Gatwick (Credit: Unsplash)
What this signals for supply chain leaders
Airlines outsourcing ground handling are essentially extending their supply chain to a third-party partner at the exact point where service failures become visible to passengers fastest. The choice of provider carries reputational weight well beyond the operational contract itself, particularly on routes like Manchester-Scandinavia, where connecting passengers have little tolerance for missed transfers.
For DHL, the SAS and Air France-KLM contracts reinforce a pattern: aviation ground handling is becoming a repeatable, scalable service line within its broader supply chain business, built on the same mobilisation playbook applied twice in under six months.
For supply chain and procurement leaders evaluating outsourced
logistics partners
more broadly, that repeatability, standing up a compliant, safety-critical operation from a standing start in 30 days, is arguably the more transferable capability than the aviation specifics themselves.
Key partner cited: SAS Scandinavian Airlines
SAS Scandinavian Airlines is Scandinavia's flag carrier, operating hubs at Copenhagen, Oslo and Stockholm airports since 1946. Hans Henrik Spangenberg serves as MD SAS Ground Handling International. The airline carries more than 25 million passengers and 55,000 tonnes of cargo a year to 135 destinations, and is a SkyTeam member.

title: Q&A: Jim Mellon, Agronomics on Food Supply Chain Risk
content:
Q&A: Jim Mellon, Agronomics on Food Supply Chain Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics, shares his thoughts on upcoming risks to the food supply chain
As rising temperatures and ongoing climate disruptors create significant risk for the food supply chain, Jim Mellon shares his thoughts on upcoming risks
Around the world, supply chains have been tested by changing weather patterns and increasing demands. Food and agriculture supply chains are particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with ongoing turbulence making harvests unpredictable.
A strong El Niño is impacting climates and supply chains around the world, with an increasing concern that it will grow to become the largest on record.
Though these events are damaging to current operations, the real concern is for the harvests in 2027, as agricultural impacts typically follow a climate event by six to 12 months.
This means we could be facing lower yields and higher prices in 2027, following unpredictable weather, record-hitting temperature heights and fertiliser disruption caused by issues in the Strait of Hormuz.
Agronomics is a company focused on investing in clean and alternative food production, moving towards
building resilience
in a critical – yet vulnerable – supply chain.
Clean food is that which is produced in controlled environments, away from pesticides, microbial contamination and insecticides. Sustainable and resource-efficient production methods are used, such as cell-cultivation and precision fermentation.
The aim is to develop supply chain and food security, alongside reducing the environmental impact of industrial agriculture.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics, about the current state of the food supply chain and how resilience can be developed.
None of this argues for sidelining traditional farming. The goal has to be to complement it, freeing land and farmers to focus on higher-value, more resilient practices rather than absorbing every shock at the root.
Jim Mellon, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Agronomics
What has been a core concern for food supply chains in recent years? Has that changed over recent months?
The conversation around food security has usually centred solely on sustainability; emissions, land use, water consumption. That's still true and vitally important – agriculture generates 17% of global greenhouse gas emissions and consumes 70% of the world's freshwater. But this year, the emphasis has shifted. The core concern has
become resilience
and supply security. The FAO's Food Price Index hit 130.7 points in April 2026, and the UK's Food and Drink Federation has revised its food inflation forecast to at least 9% by year-end. Fertiliser and energy costs have risen sharply, driven by geopolitical instability, pushing prices for UK farmers up by as much as 70%.
What we're seeing is that food price shocks no longer correct themselves, the evidence suggests they drive prices up indefinitely. So the question has moved from "can we produce enough calories globally?" to "can we guarantee reliable, and accessible supply at a national level, even under stress?"
Food supply chain resilience has become a critical concern. Credit: Unsplash
How is a strong El Niño revealing vulnerabilities in agriculture supply chains?
El Niño has returned to the Pacific, and forecasters believe it could rank among the most powerful on record, alongside 1997-98 and 2015-16. Its agricultural impact typically lags the underlying climate signal by six to twelve months, so the real pressure on yields and prices is still growing through the rest of 2026 and into 2027.
It's also landing on a system already buckling under strain from a live fertiliser crunch. Climate risk and geopolitical risk are compounding rather than operating as separate problems, and a food system built almost entirely on open fields, rainfall and stable input markets has very little, if any, protection against that.
Why are perennial crops like cocoa and coffee demonstrating structural deficits, rather than rare reactions to weather issues?
Farmers can’t replant their way out of a bad season. Soil is degrading, herds have been culled and will take years to rebuild, and perennial crops in particular carry damage forward rather than resetting. Cocoa illustrates this clearly: after a
run of deficits
driven by ageing trees, disease and erratic West African rainfall, the market has only recently rebalanced into a fragile surplus, and that recovery depends entirely on the weather holding. The underlying structural problems, low farmer incomes, thin reinvestment in irrigation, remain unresolved.
Coffee shows the same pattern, with Brazil's crop outlook now a central swing factor for the whole market. Beef tells the story from another angle:
years of drought
have pushed the US cattle herd to its smallest size in generations, and ranchers can't rebuild quickly because doing so requires feed and pasture the drought hasn't allowed. These are structural problems and the effects are already being felt.
Cocoa harvests in Africa are vulnerable to weather events. Credit: Getty
What are clean ingredients and why is producing them becoming vital in today’s world?
Clean food covers technologies like precision fermentation – which uses microbes to produce ingredients such as proteins, fats and flavouring compounds – and cell cultivation – which grows real animal and planet cells directly in bioreactors. Both remove production from agricultural land, weather conditions and the volatility of traditional farming. This is incredibly important because it allows food production to be more localised, reducing reliance on global networks and exposure to cross-border disruption.
Instead of a crop absorbing sunlight over a season, microbes and cells are fed a nutrient broth in a controlled tank, multiplying into the target ingredient in days. None of this depends on this season's rainfall, this year's fertiliser price, or the state of a shipping lane thousands of miles away. And the good news is, it's happening already. Take Clean Food Group, a UK company that has a million-litre facility in Liverpool that produces CleanOil, a palm oil alternative that requires no tropical
deforestation
and no transoceanic shipping.
Jim explains
Agriculture is responsible for 17% of global greenhouse gas emissions
70% of the world's freshwater is consumed by the agriculture sector
In April, the FAO's Food Price Index hit 130.7 points
UK farmers are facing price increases of up to 70%
What can organisations do to develop agricultural resilience in today’s modern world?
The response cannot simply be to absorb each shock and wait for it to pass, because the next one is already visible on the horizon. Organisations need to invest now in production that sits outside the climate and geopolitical risk cycle. That means treating clean food technologies as
strategic infrastructure
rather than experimental science and backing companies scaling these processes commercially. We also need companies to work with policymakers on regulatory pathways.
It’s important to caveat that none of this argues for sidelining traditional farming. The goal has to be to complement it, freeing land and farmers to focus on higher-value, more resilient practices rather than absorbing every shock at the root.

title: Capacity Gap Pushes Supply Chains Toward AI Agents
content:
Capacity Gap Pushes Supply Chains Toward AI Agents
Prioritise Us
on Google
77% of decision-makers say they have delayed or avoided a strategic initiative because their team lacked the hours to pursue it, according to IFS research (Image source: IFS Loops Agentic Platform)
New research from IFS and The Futurum Group finds enterprises are turning to agentic digital workers to close the capacity gap
Industrial organisations are losing two-fifths (66%) of employee time to manual, repetitive work, according to new research from The Futurum Group, commissioned by IFS. The study, published in August 2026, surveyed 664 enterprise decision-makers across manufacturing, energy and utilities, aerospace and defence, transportation and logistics, construction and
telecommunications
The findings point to a widening capacity gap between the work industrial organisations need to do and the actual capacity of their teams. More than three-quarters (77%) of decision-makers say they have delayed or avoided a strategic initiative because their team lacked the hours to pursue it.
For supply chain leaders, that constraint compounds an existing workforce problem. Experienced engineers and operators are retiring across factories, utilities and supply chains, taking institutional knowledge with them. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of organisations say about half or more of their
operational knowledge is undocumented
, and more than half of teams constantly or frequently repeat work because information is hard to find.
Where the gap bites hardest
The shape of the problem varies by sector, but supply chain and procurement functions feature prominently across every industry surveyed. In transportation and logistics specifically, the top three agentic AI use cases identified were knowledge and documentation support (43%), service planning (38%) and parts and
inventory management
(36%), reflecting the coordination burden of fragmented, distributed networks.
Across the six core industrial segments, the top use case in each rarely captures even half the available opportunity, meaning organisations need a platform that can orchestrate multiple processes rather than automate a single task in isolation.
Here’s a sector breakdown of the top AI use cases:
manufacturing prioritises materials planning and inventory coordination across disconnected systems
energy and utilities lean on knowledge and documentation support as their workforce ages
transportation and logistics favour carrier coordination and scheduling across distributed networks
construction focuses on resource and schedule planning to offset material delays
aerospace and defence emphasise compliance-aware operational support amid supplier delays
telecommunications prioritise dispatch automation and knowledge capture from experienced staff.
Trust, not technology, is the holdup
Despite that appetite, adoption remains cautious. Just 5.7% of decision-makers currently trust AI to act fully autonomously, even though 66% say they are likely to invest in digital workers within the next 12 months. Two-thirds of
AI projects
reach half of full production or less, and poor data quality is the most-cited reason projects stall, ahead of proving ROI or integration challenges.
Somya Kapoor, Chief Executive Officer at IFS Loops, says closing the gap requires more than general-purpose tools.
Closing it takes more than general-purpose AI. Digital workers built for the job, integrated into the systems already running the business, are what let teams reclaim capacity instead of just working around the shortfall.
Somya Kapoor, Chief Executive Officer, IFS Loops
What production deployments look like
Rather than waiting for perfect data, several IFS customers have moved digital workers into live procurement and order-to-pay workflows. At Kitron Group, an electronics manufacturer with around 3,500 employees across 13 sites in the Nordics, Poland, China and Malaysia, a digital worker rollout is on track to reach all locations by the end of 2026.
Business Application Manager Jonatan Gustafsson's team abandoned
robotic process automation
after finding every new supplier introduced its own rules, an unsustainable burden given the company's 10-15% annual growth in purchase order volume. During the rollout, the digital worker traced a part-number mismatch to a data-entry error made a decade earlier, correcting a fault a manual process had missed for years.
At Ependion, a company with around 1,000-employees that operates in 20 countries, CIO Joakim Stolt's team brought a Supply Order Manager live company-wide through a 10-week progressive rollout. Stolt frames the measure of success around time, not jobs, telling researchers the primary KPI is time saved for users rather than headcount reduction.
At Sims Crane, Chief Business Operations Officer Curtis Taylor is targeting an 80/20 straight-through rate for accounts payable, arguing that anything short of that threshold is closer to assisted data entry than genuine automation.
IFS research found that 66% are likely to invest in digital workers within the next 12 months (Credit: Getty)
Why this matters for supply chain leaders
The research points to three capabilities separating pilots that reach production from those that stall: native integration with existing systems such as ERP, EAM and FSM platforms, governance and auditability built in from the outset, and a human-in-the-loop exception model that routes only genuine exceptions to a person.
Nearly two-thirds of enterprises say they would rather buy a digital worker platform, ready-made or customised, than build one internally. For supply chain and
procurement leaders
assessing where to prioritise investment, it is not whether to deploy agentic AI but how quickly a chosen platform can move from pilot to measurable production use, since only 6.5% of organisations say more than three-quarters of their AI projects currently deliver measurable business value.
Key partner cited: IFS
IFS is an industrial AI software provider founded in 1983, headquartered with more than 7,000 employees across 80 countries. Somya Kapoor serves as Chief Executive Officer of IFS Loops, the company's agentic digital worker platform. IFS technology supports businesses that manufacture goods, maintain complex assets and manage service-focused operations.

title: BMW's new iX3 EV is racking up orders, even in China, despite selling only an image
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 27 2026 - 8:35 am PT
With global orders for the
near 100,000, BMW dealers in China are reportedly overwhelmed by demand, with tens of thousands of pre-orders coming in in less than a week after it went on sale.
The new BMW iX3 is off to a strong start, even in China
After launching the new iX3, the first from its Neue Klasse (“New Class”) lineup last September, BMW’s former CEO Oliver Zipse revealed the electric SUV
secured 50,000 orders
in its first six months on the market.
BMW said on Thursday that orders were now nearing 100,000. To meet the stronger-than-expected demand, the company added a second shift at its plant in Debrecen, Hungary, earlier this year.
While the promising start has caught even BMW off guard, the new iX3 is reportedly now drawing big interest in China, where the luxury automaker, like most foreign OEMs, is quickly losing market share to domestic EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi.
BMW launched the new iX3 in China at the Chengdu Auto Show on August 21 in three variations, with prices ranging from 269,900 yuan to 339,900 yuan ($40,200 to $50,500).
Several BMW dealers told
that “Once the pre-sale price was announced, the sales team has barely stopped working, working until 10 pm every day,” adding that “there are just too many interested users.”
Shao Bin, Senior Vice President of Marketing at BMW Brilliance Automotive Ltd at the 2026 Chengdu Auto Show (Source: BMW)
In just under a week, each BMW store in the core area has received nearly 80 “small orders,” the dealers claimed. Since it went on sale, the new BMW iX3 has reportedly secured “tens of thousands” of small blind pre-orders.
The “overwhelming demand” comes despite having essentially zero actual vehicles to show. “We’re not selling cars, we’re just selling pictures, Xiao Zhou, a BMW salesperson, told
In the 10 years that Zhou has worked for BMW, this is the first time that he has had no models to display after opening pre-sales.
BMW expects show cars will begin arriving at dealerships at the end of October, followed by the first customer deliveries in November.
BMW iX3 50L (Source: BMW)
Full-scale deliveries are not expected to begin until 2027. According to BMW’s app, those who place an order can have it confirmed by January 31, 2027.
To keep potential buyers interested, BMW introduced a new “waiting points” system, which many local EV manufacturers use. From the day they place an order, iX3 buyers will receive 100 BMW membership points a day until the vehicle is delivered.
With a total of about 16,000 points possible from now until January 2027, the value is worth around 4,000 yuan,
said, or roughly $600.
The BMW i3 Long Wheelbase (left) and iX3 Long Wheelbase (right) Source: BMW
A source close to BMW’s R&D team told
that some of the new technology included in the iX3 is still in the final stages of testing. BMW “would rather delay delivery than hand over a half-finished product to users,” the source said.
Like in Europe and other overseas markets, BMW’s new iX3 is off to a promising start in China as well.
As the first EV based on BMW’s Neue Klasse platform with its sixth-generation eDrive (Gen6) architecture, the new iX3 is a step change from its first-generation electric vehicles.
BMW iX3 50L prototype drives 500 miles in real-world driving conditions (Source: BMW)
The new BMW iX3 has an official CLTC range of up to 919 km (517 mi). In June, BMW tested an iX3 50L xDrive Long Wheelbase (LWB) prototype, which
covered over 800 km
(500 miles) around the Qinghai Lake grand loop.
BMW put it through the paces, repeatedly climbing hills with an elevation gain of over 6,500 feet (nearly 2,000 meters) and driving through “heavy snowfall, intense rain, and strong high-altitude sunshine.”
The prototype achieved an energy consumption of 20.3 kWh/100 miles (12.6 kWh/100 km), or 4.9 miles per kWh, and still had 2% battery capacity at the end of the journey.
BMW iX3 interior (China-spec) Source: BMW
BMW said that under the same real-world driving conditions, the iX3 LWB could achieve a driving range of about 835-840 km (518-522 miles).
The China-specific iX3 also features nearly 40 “high-value features” as standard on all trims, including BMW’s Panoramic iDrive, a new end-to-end autonomous driving system developed with Momenta, and a new AI-powered Intelligent Assistant with Alibaba Large Language Models (LLMs).
Electrek’s Take
Although the orders in China are blind pre-orders and likely a bit inflated, the new iX3 is still doing one thing — getting buyers interested in the brand again.
BMW still has a long way to go to revamp the brand in China, the world’s largest EV market. In the first half of 2026, BMW Group’s sales in China plummeted by 20% compared to the same period last year.
Its attention to detail has helped BMW get to where it is today, but to keep up with Chinese brands like BYD and Xiaomi, it will need to shorten its development cycle drastically. Generating hype is one thing, but converting it into actual sales is another.
In the US, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is
available to order
, starting at $61,500. It has an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles.
The BMW iX3 40 is on sale in Germany, starting at €63,400 ($73,000), with a WLTP driving range of 628 km (390 miles), while the iX3 50 xDrive is priced from €73,925 ($85,200), with a driving range of up to 805 km (500 miles).
The LWB version’s wheelbase is 108 mm longer than that of the standard iX3, but it’s specifically designed for China.

title: Waymo takes a shot at Tesla's self-driving: it's a 'false summit'
content:
Waymo published a list of “10 AI lessons” from driving more than 200 million fully autonomous miles, and several of them read as a direct rebuke of Tesla’s self-driving strategy — without ever naming Tesla.
The sharpest: trying to turn a driver-assist system into full autonomy is a “false summit,” according to Waymo. That’s exactly what Tesla is attempting with Full Self-Driving.
What Waymo actually said
The post, published Tuesday by Waymo’s head of AI foundations, Srikanth Thirumalai, frames all 10 lessons around safety and the company’s 200-million-mile record in fully driverless operation.
Lesson 10 is the one aimed squarely at the L2-to-L4 playbook:
Simply improving a driver-assist system (L2) for full autonomy is a false summit. True L4 maturity can only be safely achieved by a purpose-built system, validated on closed courses and hardened by the uncompromising experience of driving without a human in the car.
Waymo’s argument is that neither billions of simulated miles nor millions of “supervised” human-present miles can replicate what a system learns once it operates with no human backup. That’s a pointed contrast with Tesla, which trains FSD on data from a fleet of customer cars whose drivers remain legally responsible for the vehicle.
Cameras alone and the ‘black box’
Two other lessons land in Tesla’s lap.
Lesson 1 states plainly that cameras alone can’t deliver safe, full-scale autonomy, and that Waymo combines cameras, lidar, and radar for redundancy. Tesla runs a camera-only “Tesla Vision” stack — a bet Waymo’s co-CEO already picked apart earlier this month when he explained why camera-only self-driving falls short.
Lesson 4 warns against pure end-to-end neural networks that convert raw camera input directly into steering commands: “You can’t build trust with a black box.” Tesla has spent the last two years selling exactly that end-to-end approach as the core of FSD v14 and v15.
However, the approach often results in a two-step-forward, one-step-back situation with every new update.
The widening gap behind the jab
The confidence has numbers behind it. Waymo is now serving more than 500,000 paid, fully driverless rides every week across its US markets, and it has set a target of one million by the end of the year.
Tesla, by comparison, still runs a small “Robotaxi” service that launched in Austin with human safety monitors in the car, and by some counts its fleet has shrunk rather than grown. CEO Elon Musk has promised “unsupervised” FSD would be widespread by year-end — a target he has moved repeatedly.
A year into the program, Tesla confirmed last month that it has driven only 380,000 unsupervised miles – something Waymo does in a day.
Electrek’s Take
Waymo didn’t name Tesla, but it didn’t have to. Every one of these “lessons” maps onto a specific Tesla decision: camera-only sensing, an end-to-end black box, and, most pointedly, the belief that you can incrementally upgrade a consumer driver-assist product into a robotaxi.
The “false summit” line is the interesting one and should ring true to anyone following Tesla’s effort closely. CEO Elon Musk has declared victory so many times when it comes to solving autonomy and each time, it was indeed a false summit.
Top comment by JoeUser
As I’ve posted before, I live in the middle of the robotaxi service area in Austin. I see far fewer Robotaxis now than I did 6 months ago. On the plus side, they are always ‘unsupervised’, but it’s really like one a month, if that. Waymos I see a few dozen every day. If Tesla was even close to solving autonomy the fleet would be exploding. Tesla is undoubtedly winning in the ADAS arena, but they are not even close on autonomy.
Waymo is arguing that the hardest part of autonomy, the long tail of weird, dangerous edge cases, only reveals itself when there’s no human to catch the mistakes. Tesla’s approach assumes it can climb to that summit gradually, learning from millions of Teslas whose drivers are still doing the catching. Waymo is telling the market that path doesn’t reach the real peak; it just gets you to a ledge that looks like one.
Is Waymo right? I don’t know. But it is certainly ahead of Tesla and scaling much faster. Its sensor fusion approach appears much more robust than Tesla’s vision-only.
Now, Tesla fans would argue that none of that matters because Tesla is on the verge of achieving generalization and would quickly overtake Waymo, if that’s the case. But there’s no clear evidence that’s happening.

title: Storm Sondors is back, teasing mysterious new electric bike [Photo]
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 27 2026 - 5:24 am PT
Just when you thought the SONDORS story was over, Storm Sondors appears to be mounting another comeback.
The entrepreneur behind one of the most influential – and eventually most controversial – electric bike companies in the US has resurfaced with a mysterious new two-wheeler being teased on the SONDORS website.
For now, details are exceedingly thin. The ⁠SONDORS
has been stripped down to little more than a dark teaser image showing what appears to be a new moped-style electric bicycle, along with “001” and a September 3 date.
Admittedly, it doesn’t show much. But after I cranked up the exposure on that teaser image and tweaked the lighting a bit more, it’s easy to see that there are several clues hiding in the shadows.
The bike appears to feature a long bench-style saddle, relatively small and wide tires, an upright riser handlebar, and what looks like a large triangular central frame section covered by a distinctive slotted panel. There appears to be a bicycle crank and chain, suggesting at least an attempt at a landing in the three-class electric bicycle system in the US.
A substantial-looking dual crown front suspension fork is visible as well, and the overall silhouette falls squarely in the increasingly popular moped-style e-bike category. Basically, it’s pretty obvious that this will be the type of bike we have often referred to as a SUPER73 competitor, though at this point SUPER73 is likely more of a fellow member of that group of e-bikes than the leader it once was.
There simply isn’t enough visible yet to make any useful guesses about the motor, battery, performance, or even exactly how SONDORS intends to classify the vehicle. But if September 3 is indeed the reveal date, we shouldn’t have to wait long.
And perhaps the bigger story isn’t even the bike. It’s the name behind it.
The complicated history of SONDORS
Storm Sondors burst onto the electric bicycle scene
way back in 2015
with a proposition that seemed almost too good to be true: a $500 fat-tire electric bicycle.
At a time when most decent e-bikes in the US still cost several thousand dollars, the original SONDORS bike was disruptive in the truest sense of the word. The crowdfunding campaign raised millions of dollars and quickly turned SONDORS into one of the most recognizable names in the nascent US e-bike industry.
And despite plenty of early skepticism and the many detractors calling it a scam, the comapny delivered. Sure, the bikes came in late, cost a bit more than they should have, and didn’t always live up to the full specs originally promised. But they arrived. And over the following years, Sondors did something important that shouldn’t be erased by what happened later: he actually put a lot of people on electric bikes.
It’s unclear exactly how many bikes were sold under the SONDORS name over the years, but company statements and
SEC filings
put the number in at least the high five figures, if not the low six figures. Whatever number you choose SONDORS made various larger marketing claims over the years – we’re talking about tens of thousands of real electric bicycles that reached real riders.
SONDORS also helped demonstrate just how effective the direct-to-consumer model could be for inexpensive e-bikes. The company developed everything from fat-tire bikes and folders to more sophisticated models, often offering eye-catching designs at prices well below the established competition.
The original SONDORS e-bike that took the industry by “storm” in 2015
But there was another side to the SONDORS playbook.
Delays became something of a recurring theme. Products often arrived later than originally promised, and sometimes with specifications or designs that had changed along the way. For years, though, SONDORS generally managed to pull it off. As I wrote
back in 2023
, the pattern was often something along the lines of “delivered late and under-specced but always getting there. Mostly.”
SONDORS expanded into folding bikes, full-suspension bikes, scrambler-style bikes, and even crazier projects like an
ill-fated three-wheeled electric car.
Then came the Metacycle.
The Metacycle changed everything
When SONDORS
unveiled the Metacycle electric motorcycle in 2021
, it looked like another potential industry disruptor. The $5,000 motorcycle was originally pitched with an 80 mph (130 km/h) top speed and 80 miles (130 km) of range.
The motorcycle was late – very late – and the production version changed considerably from the original concept. But eventually Metacycles really did start reaching customers in 2022. By early 2023, Storm Sondors told
Electrek
that nearly 2,000 had been shipped.
I rode one myself
, and despite the missed specs and changed design, it was actually a fun little electric motorcycle.
Unfortunately, that wasn’t the end of the story.
Deliveries eventually slowed to a trickle while customers continued waiting for motorcycles and, in some cases, refunds. I later learned from SONDORS’ Chinese manufacturer, and revealed in
a detailed exposé
, that hundreds of completed Metacycles and large quantities of components were sitting in China amid a financial and contractual dispute between the factory and SONDORS. The factory accused SONDORS of failing to make required payments on bikes already shipped to him and others still in production; Storm later disputed the characterization of the situation and showed
Electrek
records of millions of dollars in payments, arguing that funds he had already paid on future orders should have been applied differently to settle current debts.
At least hundreds of paying Metacycle customers, but potentially more, were ultimately left without motorcycles, while an unknown number of SONDORS e-bike customers were also caught up in the collapse.
So… is everyone ready for SONDORS 2.0?
That’s what makes this new teaser so interesting.
Storm Sondors has always had an impressive ability to identify the kind of electric two-wheelers people want and package them in designs that generate attention. The original $500 fat-tire bike was the right product at the right moment. Even the Metacycle, for all of the disaster surrounding its rollout, was an incredibly compelling concept. It was the motorcycle that the US needed, at the moment it needed it, and at the right price. A stylish, lightweight, highway-capable electric motorcycle for around $5,000 was exactly the sort of product so many riders wanted.
The question has rarely been whether Storm can make people
the product. He’s repeatedly proved that he can.
The question this time is whether he can convince them to pay for it.
And the market he’s apparently returning to is considerably different from the one SONDORS helped create a decade ago.
Moped-style electric bikes were once a much smaller category dominated by a handful of recognizable brands, particularly SUPER73. Today, that market is packed with competitors ranging from tiny direct-to-consumer startups to established e-bike companies. Even the
reborn Juiced Bikes has returned
under new ownership with its new Scrambler lineup, offering exactly the sort of motorcycle-inspired electric bicycles that this mysterious SONDORS machine appears positioned against.
In other words, Storm isn’t coming back to an empty field.
He may still have one advantage, though: the guy knows how to get attention. I’m writing an article about a mostly black photograph of a bicycle, after all, and all because his legacy is pages longer than almost anyone else in the industry at this point.
But attention and trust aren’t the same thing.
If this new SONDORS project is going to succeed, the most convincing launch strategy should probably have less to do with outrageous specifications or an irresistible introductory price and more to do with demonstrating that finished bikes actually exist, production is funded, and customers won’t be asked to bankroll another ambitious production run with an open-ended preorder like the last few rounds of this game.
Remember, there are still tens of thousands of riders out there who had perfectly good experiences with SONDORS bikes. But on the flip side, there are also many former customers for whom the SONDORS name represents money paid for a product that never arrived.
That’s a cargo e-bike’s worth of baggage landing squarely on the rackless frame of yet another moped-style e-bike.
For now, all we’ve got is a silhouette, the number “001,” and September 3.
Whatever Storm Sondors is planning for his next act, we’ll apparently find out next week.

title: APM announces massive electrification program for Port of NY and NJ
content:
electric trucks
orange ev
Jo Borrás
| Aug 27 2026 - 5:05 am PT
96 electric terminal trucks from Orange EV, 34 electric rubber-tired gantry cranes from Konecranes, and massive investments in modernization and workforce development – and that’s just part of what APM Terminals Elizabeth is bringing to the Port of New York and New Jersey.
APM Terminals Elizabeth is a massive operation, moving nearly 30% of container traffic across the Port of New York and New Jersey and supporting more than 600 vessel calls and 800,000 truck loads each year. That kind of volume puts things like managing projections and minimizing downtime absolutely critical for the company’s long-term success – so, of course,
they are doubling down on fleet electrification
To that end, the port operator has placed orders for
96 Class 8 electric terminal tractors from Orange EV
and 34 electric rubber-tired gantry cranes from
Konecranes
. That’s
new heavy-duty electric equipment assets,
plus the associated charging infrastructure necessary to bring them online in the very near future
Konecranes eRTG
Container-handling RTG; via Konecranes.
“The future of Elizabeth depends on our willingness to invest today,” says Henrik Kristensen, Managing Director of APM Terminals Elizabeth. “These [orders] represent another important milestone in our modernization journey, helping us strengthen critical port infrastructure, enhance operational performance and prepare for future cargo growth. Modernization is about more than equipment and facilities. It is also about investing in our people. Together with our labor partners, we are building the capabilities, skills and expertise needed to support the next generation of terminal operations while keeping our workforce at the center of our success.”
As APM continues its electrification journey,
the terminal is also working to ensure its workforce is ready for its new EVs
. Working closely with regional labor partners, the operator is investing in training and operational capabilities needed to support the future of cargo handling at the Port of New York and New Jersey.

title: London police are now using the same illegal e-bikes as the criminals they chase
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Aug 27 2026 - 2:55 am PT
London police have apparently decided that if you can’t beat them, join them – or at least get yourself the same electric bike.
The Metropolitan Police has expanded its fleet of high-powered electric two-wheelers used to chase suspects across London, adding 20 new electric motorbikes and bringing the fleet to 25. The machines can reach speeds of around 50 mph (80 km/h), hop curbs, tackle stairs, and follow suspects into places where a traditional police motorcycle, electric bicycle, or squad car simply can’t go.
And judging by the photos released by Scotland Yard, those bikes are Sur-Rons – the very same type of lightweight electric dirt bikes that have become infamous for their use by criminals and illegal street riders in London.
The irony is pretty thick. Even an official Sur-Ron social media page
posted a quip
about it.
Sur-Ron-style electric motorcycles have more frequently been referred to by a new colloquialism of “e-motos,” separating it from the more longstanding colloquialism of “e-bikes” that has long encompassed a wide range of two-wheeled EVs from lightweight electric bicycles to higher powered rides. But legally speaking, these Sur-Rons are mostly just electric dirt bikes, far from anything considered road legal in the UK.
Local electrically assisted pedal cycles are limited to 250W of continuous motor power and assistance up to 15.5 mph (25 km/h). Anything exceeding those limits is generally treated as a motor vehicle and must meet the corresponding registration, insurance, licensing, and approval requirements to be legally operated on public roads.
Of course, the police bikes are presumably (or hopefully) being operated under some appropriate legal framework. The point is that unregistered Sur-Rons ridden on public streets – the same machines police routinely seize from illegal riders – are very much illegal.
In fact,
the Met itself lists
illegal e-bike use as a policing priority in parts of London, including enforcement and seizure of illegally ridden machines.
But there’s a good reason police want them.
Phone snatching has become a major problem in London, often involving thieves using fast electric bikes to approach victims and then escape through traffic, alleys, parks, and pedestrian areas. According to Reuters, reported mobile phone thefts fell from roughly 68,000 to 54,000 in the 12 months through May, though fewer than 1% of offenses currently result in what the Met calls a “positive outcome,” such as a charge or caution, according to
Police say combining the fast electric motorbikes with drones has helped officers close the mobility gap. The Met described its expanded e-bike fleet as part of its effort to target gangs using e-bikes and mopeds for crime.
, Mayor of London, said:
“The Met’s new fleet of Sur-Ron e-bikes sends a clear message that London will not tolerate criminal behaviour,” explained London Mayor Sadiq Khan in a statement. “These bikes have been successfully helping the Met to go after offenders who are increasingly using high-powered, illegally modified e-bikes to commit crimes and it’s great to be able to expand the fleet. With record funding from City Hall, the Met are using the latest innovation and technology, alongside neighbourhood policing, to stay one step ahead of criminals.”
And frankly, it makes sense. Sur-Rons became popular with criminals for many of the same reasons enthusiasts love them: they’re quick, quiet, narrow, lightweight, and ridiculously capable off-road.
Now the police chasing them finally have the same advantages.
Sometimes the best tool for catching an illegal bike is, apparently, another one.

title: SolarWindow launches 0.85 mm-thick, self-adhesive solar film - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
SolarWindow has launched ElectroFlex, an ultra-thin, flexible, self-adhesive solar product for flat and curved surfaces. The new product features 24.4% cell efficiency and targets transportation, aerospace, buildings and other weight-sensitive applications.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
27 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
US-based SolarWindow Technologies has announced the commercial launch of ElectroFlex, an ultra-thin, flexible solar product designed to generate electricity on flat and curved surfaces.
The product targets applications where conventional PV modules face limitations due to weight, rigidity, or mounting requirements.
The company describes ElectroFlex as a “peel-and-stick” solution that can be applied directly to various surfaces without frames, rigid glass, or conventional support structures. Its size and color can be customized to meet customer specifications.
The new product consists of a five-layer composite laminate measuring 0.85 mm in total thickness. The stack comprises a 0.10 mm front encapsulant, 0.16 mm high-efficiency solar cells, a 0.04 mm copper cell backing, a 0.30 mm composite laminate and a 0.25 mm rear substrate.
ElectroFlex is 0.85 mm thick and integrates interdigitated back-contact (IBC) cells with a power conversion efficiency of 24.4%, according to the manufacturer. It has a power-to-weight ratio of approximately 73 W/kg.
SolarWindow said it also supplies wiring, harnesses, electrical systems, and power-balancing components needed to integrate the product and deliver the electricity it generates.
The company is targeting applications in the transportation, marine, aerospace, architecture, agriculture, infrastructure, utility, and specialty vehicle sectors.
Potential applications include data centers and buildings, roofs of commercial trucks and fleet vehicles, curved train surfaces, and drone and aircraft structures, according to the manufacturer.
ElectroFlex is initially available to Tier 1 original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) in the United States. SolarWindow said it plans to expand sales to selected markets in North America and Asia over the coming quarters.
The company is also developing LiquidElectricity, a transparent coating designed to turn glass and plastic surfaces into electricity-generating elements. SolarWindow claims the technology, which remains under development, could generate electricity from natural and artificial light, as well as low-intensity, shaded, and reflected light.

title: Battery boom brings round-the-clock solar closer, Ember says - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar PV supplied more than 10% of global electricity in the first half of 2026, but generation remains heavily concentrated around midday. Ember says rapidly expanding, cheaper battery storage could shift 34% of new daily solar generation to non-solar hours in 2026, bringing round-the-clock solar closer.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
27 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
A study by British energy think tank Ember suggests that the prospect of round-the-clock solar photovoltaic (PV) availability is drawing closer. Solar PV generated just over 10% of global electricity in the first half of 2026, up from 8.9% in the same period of 2025. Its share has nearly doubled from the 5.6% recorded in the first half of 2023.
Over the past three years, solar PV generation has grown seven times faster than total electricity generation. While global electricity generation rose by 12% between the first half of 2023 and the first half of 2026, solar generation more than doubled, from 769 TWh to 1,564 TWh.
However, this growth remains heavily concentrated around midday. On an average day in the first half of 2026, solar met more than 25% of global electricity demand between 11:00 and 14:00, before falling to near-zero levels between 20:00 and 05:00.
In markets with higher levels of solar PV penetration, this concentration is even more pronounced. In Chile, where solar met 26% of electricity demand in the first half of 2026, its contribution reached 71% at midday but had virtually disappeared by 21:00. In the Netherlands, solar met 58% of demand at 13:00, while in Germany it covered 55% at midday. In both markets, however, solar’s contribution fell to zero a few hours later.
Fossil-fuel generation maintains its position after sunset
The expansion of solar PV is displacing fossil-fuel generation during the day, but hours without sunlight remain a key domain for conventional generation. Between the first half of 2023 and the first half of 2026, average fossil-fuel generation between 11:00 and 14:00 fell from 86 GW to 69 GW. During the evening peak, between 19:00 and 21:00, however, the decline was much smaller, from 106 GW to 101 GW.
New battery storage installations in 2026 are projected to reach 459 GWh, up 50% from the 307 GWh added in 2025. According to Ember data, this capacity could theoretically shift 34% of new daily solar generation to non-solar hours.
This proportion is nearly double the 18% estimated for batteries installed in 2025 and compares with just 4% five years earlier, in 2021.
Falling battery installation costs have been a key driver of this progress. Average global costs fell by 95% between 2010 and 2025, from $2,634/kWh to $140/kWh.
Bulgaria and Chile lead the rollout
While batteries installed globally in 2025 could shift the equivalent of 18% of new daily solar generation, some countries achieved significantly higher shares.
Bulgaria installed enough storage to shift 77% of its new daily solar generation, followed by Chile at 76% and Australia at 60%.
Bulgaria’s growth has been particularly rapid. The country went from virtually no battery storage capacity in 2023 to adding around 3 GWh in 2025. By May 2026, installed capacity had surpassed 8.6 GWh.
Chile followed a similar trajectory, adding 4 GWh of battery storage in 2025 and bringing its installed capacity to 7.6 GWh. Most of the new storage was installed alongside solar plants, helping to reduce curtailment and shift solar generation into the evening hours.
The United States added 58 GWh of storage in 2025, enough to shift approximately one-quarter of its new daily solar generation.
The European Union, meanwhile, added 27 GWh of battery storage in 2025, equivalent to shifting 16% of new daily solar generation and below the global average.
Solar power begins to extend into the evening
In California, the combination of solar and battery storage met more than a quarter of electricity demand during the evening peak, between 19:00 and 21:00, on an average day in the first half of 2026. In the first half of 2023, the figure stood at 6.8%.
In the first half of 2026, batteries enabled solar energy to meet more than 10% of evening electricity demand in Chile. In Bulgaria, solar and storage together covered nearly a quarter (24%) of electricity demand between 19:00 and 21:00 and supplied an average of 10% of demand between 19:00 and 07:00.
However, developing solar generation capable of supplying electricity beyond daylight hours will require more than additional battery capacity. Electricity markets must also enable batteries to participate effectively and operate where they provide the greatest value to the power system.
Ember concludes that batteries do not eliminate the need for a diversified electricity mix. Wind, hydropower, nuclear power, and long-duration energy storage will continue to play significant roles, particularly during extended periods of low solar or wind generation.

title: Executive order bans foreign-produced transformers, inverters, and circuit breakers for U.S. power grid - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
President Donald Trump issued an emergency executive order banning the acquisition, importation, transfer, or installation of foreign-produced electrical grid equipment from designated foreign countries, according to a legal analysis published by law firm Norton Rose Fulbright.
Ryan Kennedy
27 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Inverters
United States
Utility-scale
A newly issued
executive order by President Donald Trump
restricts foreign-made electrical infrastructure across the United States bulk-power system, taking direct aim at equipment connected to entities in 24 embargoed nations. The action targets high-voltage hardware including transformers, utility-scale inverters, circuit breakers, energy storage systems, and industrial control electronics, citing concerns over potential remote access, cyber vulnerabilities, and grid disruption.
While the executive order technically applies to transactions initiated after Aug. 26, 2026, Norton Rose Fulbright noted in its analysis that equipment is not formally barred until the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) evaluates specific vendors and issues official risk determinations.
The DOE has 120 days (until Dec. 24, 2026) to publish formal rules implementing the policy. However, the agency is instructed to make recommendations to the National Security Council to isolate, monitor, or replace sensitive infrastructure as soon as practicable.
According to law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, the executive action applies broadly to foreign-produced equipment used in substations, power generation facilities, and control rooms tied to the bulk-power system. While transmission lines rated at 69 kV or higher are explicitly included, the order also covers generation assets necessary to maintain overall power system reliability.
The specific hardware covered spans power conversion and storage, substation and transmission equipment, and generation and control systems. This includes utility-scale and grid-connected inverters, battery energy storage systems, and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units. It also encompasses substation transformers, high-voltage circuit breakers, voltage regulators, capacitors, instrument transformers, and automated reclosers. In addition, the scope covers industrial and distributed control systems, remote terminal units (RTUs), programmable logic controllers (PLCs), generation turbines, and their associated software and firmware.
The order excludes residential or commercial distributed energy assets that connect solely to local low-voltage distribution lines.
Restrictions apply to equipment designed, manufactured, or supplied by vendors tied to 24 designated sanction- and arms-embargoed countries under U.S. International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR).
While the list includes nations such as Iran, Russia, and Syria, China represents the primary commercial supplier affected across solar, battery, and electrical component supply chains.
Norton Rose Fulbright noted that the DOE may establish a pre-qualified vendor white-list or create a licensing framework for utilities seeking to deploy sensitive components. Regulatory mechanisms could also force asset owners to isolate, monitor, or remove previously installed gear, though any mandate would likely be phased in to maintain grid stability.
According to Norton Rose Fulbright, the executive order adds another layer of regulatory complexity for clean energy developers already navigating Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions, domestic content rules, Section 45X manufacturing credits, and import tariffs.

title: Ireland’s PV capacity reaches 3 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
“With continued investment in solar – across homes, farms, businesses and large grid-scale projects – Ireland is building a growing source of homegrown, clean electricity, and strengthening our energy security,” said Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, Darragh O’Brien following the milestone.
Blathnaid O’Dea
27 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Ireland has passed 3 GW of installed solar capacity, according to Irish PV association Solar Ireland. This comes from both large utility-scale sites and rooftop installations, according to the industry association.
“Three gigawatts is a big moment for Irish solar,” said Ronan Power, CEO, Solar Ireland, pointing out that a lot of progress has been made in a relatively short time as Ireland’s first utility-scale solar farm was connected to the grid in 2022.
“Four years later, we have more than 200,000 homes with solar on their roofs, businesses generating their own electricity and solar power plants capable of supplying more than a third of national electricity demand at peak,” said Power.
“There has been huge investment and commitment behind that growth from Government, industry, communities and everyone involved in getting these projects connected,” he added.
The few hundred megawatts required to take Ireland to the 3 GW mark were only realized in the past few weeks as the last official statement from the government on installation numbers put the figure at 2.6 GW and this was in June.
According to Central Statistics Office figures, grid-scale solar farms
generated 1.1 GWh
of Ireland’s electricity in 2025 – a 51% increase compared to 2024.
The country’s solar industry remains set on the 2030 target of 8 GW of installed solar capacity. Developers are preparing for the sixth renewable energy auction, RESS 6, due in December. It is the first auction to incorporate the European Union’s new rules around non-price criteria under the Net Zero Industry Act (NZIA).
Speaking to
pv magazine
this week, Solar Ireland’s policy manager
Leanne Donovan
said solar is expected to compete well, but it is too soon to predict how things will turn out.
The organization is lobbying the government to ensure solar, battery energy storage and grid updates are included in the upcoming national budget for 2027.
Power said Budget 2027 needs to unlock the full value of the solar that Irish developers have spent the past few years building.
Following the 3 GW announcement, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, Darragh O’Brien, pledged to continue investing in solar.
“With continued investment in solar – across homes, farms, businesses and large grid-scale projects – Ireland is building a growing source of homegrown, clean electricity, and strengthening our energy security,” he said.
The distribution systems operator, ESB Networks, is delivering the government’s investment program of grid infrastructure upgrades.
